ap_physics_c_electricity_and_magnetism-f.title: Electric field on the axis of a charged ring

stimulus.description: A thin ring of radius $R=15\text{ cm}$ carries a charge of $Q=6\text{ nC}$ spread uniformly around it. Point P is on the axis of the ring, perpendicular to the plane of the ring through its center, at a distance $x=20\text{ cm}$ from the center. Use $k=9.0\times10^{9}\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}^{2}/\text{C}^{2}$.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: On the dot below, which represents point P, draw arrows that show the electric field at P caused by two small charge elements on opposite sides of the ring, and draw the direction of the net field at P. Each arrow must start on the dot and be labeled.
parts.model_answer: Two arrows from P pointing away from the two elements (each tilted away from the axis), whose components perpendicular to the axis cancel, and a net-field arrow along the axis pointing away from the ring.

rubric_rows.criterion: Draws two field arrows at P, each pointing away from its (positive) charge element along the line joining them
required_elements: two arrows pointing away from the elements
common_errors: draws the arrows toward the ring

rubric_rows.criterion: The two arrows have equal length and are symmetric about the axis
common_errors: draws arrows of unequal length for symmetric elements

rubric_rows.criterion: Labels the net field along the axis, pointing away from the ring, because the perpendicular components cancel
required_elements: net field along the axis away from the ring
common_errors: draws the net field perpendicular to the axis

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the magnitude of the electric field at P in terms of $k$, $Q$, $R$ and $x$.
parts.model_answer: $dE=k\,dq/(x^2+R^2)$ and only the axial component $dE\,x/\sqrt{x^2+R^2}$ survives; integrating over the ring gives $E=kQx/(x^2+R^2)^{3/2}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Writes the field of a charge element, $dE=k\,dq/(x^2+R^2)$
common_errors: uses $k\,dq/x^2$

rubric_rows.criterion: Takes the axial component with the factor $x/\sqrt{x^2+R^2}$
common_errors: omits the component factor

rubric_rows.criterion: Integrates over the ring ($\int dq=Q$) to obtain $E=kQx/(x^2+R^2)^{3/2}$
common_errors: obtains $kQ/(x^2+R^2)$

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Calculate the magnitude of the electric field at P for the given values.
parts.model_answer: $E=kQx/(x^2+R^2)^{3/2}\approx691\text{ N/C}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Substitutes the values, converting centimeters and nanocoulombs to SI units, into the expression from part B
common_errors: leaves the distances in centimeters

rubric_rows.criterion: Obtains about 691 with units of newtons per coulomb (accept any value within 2 percent)

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: The ring is replaced by a ring of the same charge but twice the radius, and point P stays at the same position. By what factor does the magnitude of the electric field at P change? Justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: The field decreases by a factor of about $0.33$: using $E=kQx/(x^2+(2R)^2)^{3/2}$ gives $230\text{ N/C}$, because the charge is farther from P and the axial component factor is smaller.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the field decreases to about 0.33 times its original value (accept any value within 3 percent)
common_errors: states that the field is unchanged because the charge is the same
states that the field is halved

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies by using $E=kQx/(x^2+R^2)^{3/2}$ with $R\to2R$ (the elements are farther away and the field is not simply inversely proportional to $R$)
common_errors: argues only that a bigger ring weakens the field without using the expression

ap_physics_c_electricity_and_magnetism-f.title: Field of a uniformly charged sphere: graph, Gauss's law and potential difference

stimulus.description: A solid nonconducting sphere of radius $R=20\text{ cm}$ carries a total charge $Q=12\text{ nC}$ spread uniformly through its volume. The sphere is in vacuum. Use $k=9.0\times10^{9}\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}^{2}/\text{C}^{2}$. Blank axes are provided on the answer sheet.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: On the axes provided, sketch the magnitude of the electric field $E$ as a function of the distance $r$ from the center of the sphere, for $0\le r\le3R$. Label the value of the field at $r=R$ in terms of $k$, $Q$ and $R$.
parts.model_answer: A straight line from the origin rising to $kQ/R^2$ at $r=R$, then a curve falling as $1/r^2$ (equal to one quarter of the peak at $r=2R$).

rubric_rows.criterion: Axes are labeled with quantities and units
The field rises linearly from zero at the center to $r=R$
common_errors: draws a field that is zero everywhere inside as for a conductor

rubric_rows.criterion: The field is continuous at $r=R$ with the labeled value $kQ/R^2$
common_errors: places the peak at a different radius

rubric_rows.criterion: Beyond $R$ the field decreases as $1/r^2$ (about one quarter of the peak at $2R$)
common_errors: draws a linear decrease

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Use Gauss's law to derive an expression for the magnitude of the electric field inside the sphere, at a distance $r<R$ from the center, in terms of $k$, $Q$, $R$ and $r$.
parts.model_answer: A spherical Gaussian surface of radius $r$ encloses $Q(r/R)^3$, so $E\,4\pi r^2=Q(r/R)^3/\varepsilon_0$ and $E=kQr/R^3$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Chooses a concentric spherical Gaussian surface and writes the flux $E\,4\pi r^2$
common_errors: uses a cylindrical Gaussian surface

rubric_rows.criterion: Finds the enclosed charge $Q(r/R)^3$ from the uniform density
common_errors: uses the whole charge $Q$ as the enclosed charge

rubric_rows.criterion: Obtains $E=kQr/R^3$
common_errors: obtains $kQ/r^2$

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Calculate the magnitude of the potential difference between the center of the sphere and its surface.
parts.model_answer: $|\Delta V|=\int_0^R kQr/R^3\,dr=kQ/(2R)\approx270.0\text{ V}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Sets up $\Delta V=-\int E\,dr$ with the interior field from part B
common_errors: uses the exterior field $kQ/r^2$ inside

rubric_rows.criterion: Integrates to obtain $kQ/(2R)$
common_errors: obtains $kQ/R$

rubric_rows.criterion: Obtains about 270.0 with units of volts (accept any value within 2 percent)

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: A second sphere has twice the radius and twice the total charge of the first (uniform volume charge). By what factor does the magnitude of the electric field at its surface differ from that at the surface of the first sphere? Justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: The field at the surface is $kQ/R^2$; doubling both $Q$ and $R$ gives $2/4=1/2$, so the surface field is half as large.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the surface field is one half of the original
common_errors: states that the field is doubled
states that the field is unchanged

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies with $E_{surface}=kQ/R^2$, with the factor $2$ from the charge and $1/4$ from the radius
common_errors: argues only that a larger charge gives a larger field

ap_physics_c_electricity_and_magnetism-f.title: Experiment: capacitance from the discharge of a capacitor

stimulus.description: A student charges a capacitor of unknown capacitance $C$ to a potential difference of about $12\text{ V}$ and then discharges it through a resistor of resistance $R=20\text{ k}\Omega$. A voltmeter connected across the capacitor is read at intervals of $10\text{ ms}$ after the discharge starts.

notes: A student charges a capacitor of unknown capacitance $C$ to a potential difference of about $12\text{ V}$ and then discharges it through a resistor of resistance $R=20\text{ k}\Omega$. A voltmeter connected across the capacitor is read at intervals of $10\text{ ms}$ after the discharge starts.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Describe an experimental procedure to collect the data for the capacitor voltage as a function of time during the discharge. Include the equipment and the measurements, how the independent variable is controlled, and one way to reduce the uncertainty in the voltage readings.
parts.model_answer: Charge the capacitor from a source, then close a switch to discharge it through the known resistor; read the voltmeter across the capacitor at equal time intervals measured with a stopwatch or record it with a data logger; use a high-impedance voltmeter so it does not discharge the capacitor, and repeat the run and average the readings.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies the circuit (charged capacitor, known resistor, switch) and a voltmeter across the capacitor read at known times
required_elements: capacitor, resistor and voltmeter across the capacitor
common_errors: places the voltmeter in series with the capacitor

rubric_rows.criterion: Controls the time by reading at equal intervals (with a timer or data logger) while keeping $R$ and $C$ the same
Reduces the uncertainty by repeating the run and averaging, or by using a high-impedance voltmeter or a data logger (any one earns the point)
required_elements: repeat and average or high-impedance voltmeter or data logger (any one earns the point)

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: For a discharging capacitor $V=V_0e^{-t/RC}$. Identify the quantities that should be plotted on the vertical and horizontal axes so that the data produce a straight line whose slope can be used to determine $C$.
parts.model_answer: Taking the natural logarithm gives $\ln V=\ln V_0-t/(RC)$: plot $\ln V$ on the vertical axis against $t$ on the horizontal axis; the slope is $-1/(RC)$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies $\ln V$ (vertical) versus $t$ (horizontal), with slope $-1/(RC)$
common_errors: plots V versus t

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: On a blank grid whose scale you choose, plot the data in the form identified in part B and draw a best-fit line. Label the axes with quantities and units and use a scale that fills most of the grid.

rubric_rows.criterion: Axes are labeled with quantities and units and the scale fills most of the grid
common_errors: scale uses less than half the grid

rubric_rows.criterion: Plots the six points $(t,\ln V)$ accurately
Draws a straight best-fit line with a negative slope through the trend of the points
common_errors: connects the dots

parts.label: D

stimulus.description: A conducting rod of length $L=1\text{ m}$ slides at constant speed $v=5\text{ m/s}$ along two parallel, frictionless conducting rails connected at one end by a resistor $R=4\,\Omega$. A uniform magnetic field of magnitude $B=0.5\text{ T}$ is perpendicular to the plane of the rails. The rod and the rails have negligible resistance.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: A student claims that no external force is needed to keep the rod moving at constant speed, because the net force on an object moving at constant velocity is zero and the rails are frictionless. Do you agree or disagree with the claim? Justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: Disagree. The motion induces an emf and a current in the circuit, and the magnetic force on that current opposes the motion (Lenz's law), so an external force equal and opposite to it is needed to keep the net force zero.

rubric_rows.criterion: Disagrees with the claim
common_errors: agrees because the speed is constant

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies the claim by explaining that the motion changes the flux, inducing an emf and a current in the rod
common_errors: says there is no current because the speed is constant

rubric_rows.criterion: Explains that the magnetic force on the induced current opposes the motion, so an external force of equal magnitude is needed
common_errors: says the magnetic force is in the direction of the motion

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the magnitude of the external force needed to keep the rod moving at constant speed in terms of $B$, $L$, $v$ and $R$, and calculate its value.
parts.model_answer: $\varepsilon=BLv$, $I=\varepsilon/R$ and $F=ILB=B^2L^2v/R\approx0.312\text{ N}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Writes the motional emf $\varepsilon=BLv$ and the current $I=\varepsilon/R$
common_errors: writes the emf as $Bv/L$

rubric_rows.criterion: Writes the magnetic force on the rod $F=ILB$ and obtains $F=B^2L^2v/R$
common_errors: obtains $B^2Lv/R$

rubric_rows.criterion: Obtains about 0.312 with units of newtons (accept any value within 2 percent)

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: The rod is now pulled at twice the speed. By what factor does the power supplied by the external force change? Justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: The force is proportional to $v$ and the power $P=Fv$ is proportional to $v^2$, so the power increases by a factor of 4 (from $1.56\text{ W}$ to $6.25\text{ W}$).

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the power increases by a factor of 4
common_errors: states that the power doubles
states that the power is unchanged

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies with $P=Fv$ and $F\propto v$, or with $P=\varepsilon^2/R$ and $\varepsilon\propto v$
common_errors: argues only that faster motion needs more power
